title: Value-Informed Schedule Trimming for Accelerated Sequential Monte Carlo Guidance in Discrete Diffusion
abstract: Reward-guided discrete diffusion enables test-time alignment with downstream objectives, but applying Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) guidance at every denoising step is computationally expensive. Active guidance steps require additional reward evaluations and, for gradient-based proposals, value-gradient computations. Sparse guidance reduces this cost by guiding only a subset of timesteps, but commonly used schedules are fixed heuristics whose effectiveness can vary substantially across tasks. We propose VISTA, a training-free method that automatically selects guided timesteps under a fixed budget. VISTA formulates sparse guidance as approximation of the ideal full-guidance probability path and derives an estimable upper bound on \(\ell_1\) path deviation. Using value statistics collected from a small number of full-guidance warmup generations, VISTA optimizes the resulting empirical surrogate exactly via dynamic programming. The warmup generations can be retained as model outputs, and after schedule selection VISTA has the same per-generation guidance complexity as other sparse schedules with the same budget. Across text, biological sequence, and image generation tasks, VISTA discovers task-dependent schedules and outperforms hand-designed sparse schedules in most tested settings, while approaching or exceeding full-guidance performance on several task metrics. In toxic-text generation, for example, VISTA attains a 0.99 unique-toxic ratio compared with 1.00 for full guidance while reducing post-selection per-generation latency from 204.23 s to 38.16 s, a 5.35$\times$ speedup.

title: Reducing the Gap Between Spatial and Space-Filling Curve Neighbors in 3D Point Cloud Segmentation
abstract: As a lightweight and highly accurate method for nearest-neighbor search in 3D point clouds, approaches based on space-filling curves (SFC) have been proposed. However, due to the inherent properties of SFC, a gap arises between proximity relationships along the SFC and those in the original Euclidean space. In this study, we propose a loss function that reduces the influence of this gap. Specifically, we compute the distances between adjacent points along the SFC and train the model to optimize feature similarity between pairs of points that are distant from each other in the original 3D space. We incorporate the proposed method into a high-performing 3D point cloud segmentation model and evaluate its effectiveness on three datasets. The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms conventional methods on both indoor and outdoor point cloud datasets.

We incorporate the proposed method into a high-performing 3D point cloud segmentation model and evaluate its effectiveness on three datasets. The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms conventional methods on both indoor and outdoor point cloud datasets.

title: AURELIANO - A Human–AI Hybrid Operational Framework for Decision Intelligence Context Management and Human
abstract: The increasing availability of generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems has expanded the possibilities for developing personalized, context-sensitive forms of human–AI collaboration. The effectiveness of such collaborations depends not only on the capabilities of the underlying language model but also on the organization of interaction, the management of contextual information, the consistency of operational rules, the verification of outputs and the allocation of decision-making authority. This paper presents Aureliano, an experimental Human–AI Hybrid Hub (HAHH) framework designed to structure these dimensions within an existing generative AI environment. Rather than introducing a new foundational model, Aureliano operates as a higher-level cognitive and procedural framework that organizes the interaction between a human principal and a general-purpose AI system. Its central objectives are to improve contextual continuity, mitigate semantic drift and entropy, distinguish evidence from inference, support complex reasoning, maintain decision traceability and preserve human authority over consequential decisions. The framework is examined through a conceptual architecture, an operational state-management model, a structured epistemic classification scheme, a human-in-the-loop validation mechanism and an exploratory verification approach. Particular attention is devoted to the distinction between persistent information and autonomous memory, between behavioral consistency and model identity and between internally reported test results and independently reproducible empirical evidence. The analysis suggests that a substantial part of the practical value of personalized AI collaboration may be produced by the systematic organization of the human–AI interface rather than by modifications to the underlying model. Nevertheless, this proposition requires controlled empirical evaluation. The paper therefore distinguishes the framework's specified properties, reported experimental observations and unresolved hypotheses. The contribution is a transferable conceptual approach to the design and evaluation of human-controlled, context-aware AI collaboration, with implications for decision support, knowledge management, organizational analysis and responsible AI governance.

title: Is learning difficulty just missing prerequisites?
abstract: A short conjecture note proposing that, with an appropriate decomposition of knowledge, every elementary learning unit has the same expected acquisition cost once its prerequisites are mastered. It discusses the limits of an existing learning system, the risk of a circular definition of ideal decomposition, and a possible empirical test. The conjecture is unproven. The conjecture is mine. AI helped turn it into words.

title: The Symbolactuality Paradox (SAP)
abstract: AbstractThe Symbolactuality Paradox (SAP) proposes a candidate domain-independent systemic principle concerning situations in which a system produces a symbolic, linguistic, representational, or otherwise surface-level marker associated with an intended outcome without thereby realizing the corresponding functional state. The originating case is an instructional interaction in which an intended diagram insertion is represented by an output such as a placement label or completion marker rather than by the functional realization of the requested diagram.The central distinction is therefore not between artificial and human systems, nor between one particular task and another, but between representation and realization. The candidate mechanism is expressed asRequirement → Symbolic/Representational Completion \neq Functional Realization.The associated apparent-completion relation isApparent Completion \neq Actual Completion.The paper develops a three-layer architecture. The first layer preserves the originating case at the philosophical-epistemological level. The second translates the distinction into systemic and cybernetic variables. The third constructs an operational mathematical framework in which criterion-specific divergence between representation and realization can be measured. A general system state is represented by t, with discrete dynamics t+1 = F(t, u, \theta) or continuous dynamics \dot{t} = F(t, u, t, \theta). The principal candidate observable is \Delta_{SA} = D_{C}(R(C, M, I), F(C, M, I)).The framework is explicitly presented as a candidate principle rather than as an established universal law. Its empirical status depends on operationalization, preregistered predictions where appropriate, counterexample testing, synthetic simulation, and cross-domain validation. The manuscript provides a 38-case validation architecture, while distinguishing documented observations from synthetic illustrative data. The mathematical formulation is intended to function as a measurement and testing architecture rather than as decorative formalism.

title: Initial and final keyword lists
abstract: The final set of publications was then scanned for mentions of technologies in order to establish a baseline collection of technology keywords. Again, the corpus was too large to complete examine manually, so the Mistral LLM was used to search for mentions of technologies. The LLM was given the title and abstract of each publication in the corpus in turn with instructions to “extract any technologies mentioned in those papers” (full system prompt in section A.1). For the purposes of this analysis, I considered a technology to be any of: programming languages, software tools/libraries, hardware or hardware platforms, and named conceptual or algorithmic frameworks the authors applied as part of their method. I took a broad stance for the definition of technology with the dual intention of a) not eliminating anything that could be useful for further analysis and b) being able to manually review and cull the list generated by the LLM. The 17,476 results returned by the LLM did feature a large number of duplicates, either as explicit duplicates, or as ontological duplicates or subsumption redundancies; as well as spurious entries arising as either a misidentification of a technology by the LLM or from publications that passed the previous filter step but were not dealing with automated assessment of training and education. I used the Python’s rapidfuzz with a conservative similarity setting of 90% and regular expressions libraries to condense duplicates and near duplicates (plurals, acronyms, and highly similar words) into single entries, resulting in 11,560 technology keywords. I then culled spurious entries by removing all items with less than 20 mentions across the corpus, reducing 11,560 keywords to 1,907. With the keyword list now tractable for human review, I then manually removed any keywords unrelated to automated assessment or too broad to be useful, resulting in a final list of 455 technology keywords relevant to automated assessment.The final step was to flatten subsumption redundancies and create a taxonomy that mapped the keywords to a useful classification system for analysis. I used a set of mutually exclusive hierarchical categories with a most-specific-level coding rule (assigning each item to the most specific category it qualifies for, falling back to a broader/residual category if no finer one applies) with NEC (Not Elsewhere Classified) residual categories at each level of generality, to code the 458 technology keywords into 13 categories deemed useful for our analysis: LLM, Natural Language Processing, Deep Learning, Machine Learning, Artificial Intelligence, Rules-Based Systems, Statistical Assessment Tools, Educational Data Mining, Blockchain, Intelligent Tutoring Systems, Massive Open Online Course, Multiple Choice Questions, and General Automated Assessment Concepts.

title: Data Structures in Python
abstract: This chapter provides a comprehensive introduction to Python’s core data structures, focusing on their creation, manipulation, and practical applications. It begins with lists, versatile and mutable data types that support operations like indexing, slicing, appending, reversing, and sorting. This chapter demonstrates these through clear examples, such as list comprehensions for filtering and transforming data (e.g., generating cubes or filtering positive/negative numbers), and highlights common pitfalls like mismatched variable assignments during unpacking. It also introduces the split() function for string-to-list conversion and the Counter class for word frequency analysis, emphasizing Python’s flexibility in handling heterogeneous data. This chapter progresses to vectors and matrices, illustrating vector operations such as addition, subtraction, dot products, and matrix manipulation through nested loops for initialization and computation. Queues are introduced as FIFO structures, with examples using the deque class, while tuples are presented as immutable lists, showcasing their creation and limitations. Sets are explored for their ability to handle unique elements and support set-theoretic operations like union and intersection, with efficient O(1) lookup. Dictionaries, as key-value hash tables, are covered extensively, including creation, iteration, and methods like get() and items(), with advanced features like OrderedDict for maintaining insertion order and defaultdict for complex data structures. This chapter concludes with a brief exploration of functional programming concepts, such as user-defined functions with *args and **kwargs for flexible argument handling, and serialization using the pickle module for data persistence. It also distinguishes between mutable (lists, dictionaries, sets) and immutable (strings, tuples, integers) types, with examples like string concatenation to illustrate immutability constraints. Additional sequence types like bytearray and xrange are mentioned, alongside techniques like enumeration and sequence unpacking, providing a solid foundation for Python’s data manipulation capabilities. This chapter equips readers with practical skills for working with Python’s data structures, supported by clear code examples and error-handling insights. By covering both basic operations and advanced techniques like comprehensions and dictionary sorting, it prepares readers for deeper exploration in subsequent chapters, particularly in applying these structures to DeepSeek and other computational tasks.

title: Task-Centric Multimodal Learning for Cognitive Impairment Detection
abstract: Dementia affects millions of older adults worldwide, yet early detection remains difficult outside clinical settings. Traditional models primarily rely on text or voice-based responses, capturing only a limited view of human cognition despite the inherently multimodal nature of human expression. This work proposes a contactless, multimodal screening framework that leverages video, audio, and text signals collected during structured voice-based interactions with Amazon Alexa. By incorporating these modalities, our approach captures a more holistic representation of human behavior encompassing speech patterns, vocal characteristics, facial expressions, and linguistic structure, which may enable more accurate detection of cognitive decline. Different participants completed three conversational tasks designed to probe spontaneous speech, comprehension, and recall. We pursued three objectives: (1) evaluate which of the three Alexa tasks provides the most informative cognitive signals, (2) compare the effectiveness of unimodal models, and (3) assess the benefits of multimodal fusion models. Task-level analysis shows that the video model achieves its best performance on Command-Reading, with an accuracy of 0.65 (AUC 0.69), while the audio model performs best on Question-Answering, reaching an accuracy of 0.67 (AUC 0.73). In contrast, the multimodal model demonstrates consistently stable performance across tasks, achieving an accuracy of 0.76 (AUC 0.75) on Command-Reading and 0.76 (AUC 0.73) on Question-Answering. These findings demonstrate that multimodal behavioral cues captured through naturalistic interactions can reliably distinguish MCI from healthy aging, highlighting the limitations of traditional diagnostic paradigms and supporting the shift toward multimodal, real-world cognitive assessment frameworks.

title: Complementary Future Token Pruning for World Action Models
abstract: World action models (WAMs) jointly predict future visual states and robot actions, but processing dense future-frame tokens incurs substantial inference latency. We propose CF-Prune, a training-free framework for pruning future-frame tokens in pretrained WAMs. Our key insight is that future visual predictions support action generation and therefore need not preserve every visual detail required for high-fidelity video synthesis. CF-Prune combines instruction and action attention to identify task-relevant tokens during the initial denoising forward pass, even when future-frame and action representations remain highly noisy. An entropy-based phase identification mechanism further retains dense computation during precision phases to mitigate pruning-induced performance degradation. Experiments on RoboLab, RoboCasa, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate consistent inference speedups. At a 35% pruning ratio, CF-Prune achieves average speedups of 1.19-1.27x while improving task success rates. At a 50% pruning ratio, it achieves 1.29-1.33x average speedups on both simulation benchmarks, with overall success rates within 1.0 percentage point of the baseline.

title: ProtModernBERT: Compute-Efficient Protein Language Modeling
abstract: Large protein language models provide a powerful framework for learning sequence-function relationships and guiding experimental design. However, architectural improvements are underexplored, especially in low-compute regimes of relevance for resource-constrained research laboratories. We show that the training cost for encoder-only transformer architectures can be reduced by leveraging modern architectural refinements, offering an encouraging performance / compute-efficiency trade-off. We introduce ProtModernBERT, a modernized BERT-style model pre-trained on amino acid sequences, and compare it with ProtBert, Amplify, and ESM2 across a set of supervised structural tasks -encompassing secondary structure prediction, disorder prediction, and subcellular localization- and ProteinGym's zero-shot functional benchmark. We find that ProtModernBERT matches or closely tracks the performance of Amplify-120M and ProtBert with up to 80-90\% reduction in pre-training FLOPs, and narrows the gap to ESM2 when controlling for pre-training. Our analysis using a cluster-based validation protocol for hyperparameter selection and randomly initialized models disentangles the contributions of architecture and data, showing that modern components provide stronger inductive biases that are more consequential than parameter count in low-compute regimes.

title: Inteligencia artificial y marketing digital: reflexiones comparadas entre Colombia y panamá a partir del periplo internacional 2025
abstract: La inteligencia artificial (IA) ha dejado de ser una herramienta emergente, para consolidarse como un motor central de innovación tecnológica en el marketing digital; a nivel global, este sector proyecta superar los 107.500 millones de dólares en 2028, con un crecimiento sostenido impulsado por algoritmos predictivos, automatización y personalización. Sin embargo, la adopción en América Latina presenta matices, en Colombia, cerca del 59 % de los consumidores interactúa cotidianamente con aplicaciones de IA, mientras que en Panamá el avance ha sido mayor debido a la inversión en infraestructura digital y políticas de innovación. Este ensayo analiza la relevancia de la IA en el marketing digital desde un enfoque comparativo, integrando cifras recientes, estudios de caso y reflexiones críticas; donde se plantea que, aunque la IA fortalece la personalización, la eficiencia y la optimización de campañas, su impacto depende de superar retos organizacionales, culturales y éticos.

title: Sparse-QITE: Discovering Compact Generators for Quantum Imaginary-Time Evolution via Regularization Methods
abstract: Quantum imaginary-time evolution (QITE) provides a systematic route to ground-state preparation, but its cost grows rapidly with the locality $D$ of the unitary approximation, for which the local Pauli basis scales as $4^D$. We introduce Sparse-QITE, a regularized formulation that promotes compact generators, reducing the number of quantum operations and yielding circuits with fewer gates and lower depth. We derive rigorous bounds on the sparsification error and benchmark the method in one-dimensional transverse-field Ising and antiferromagnetic Heisenberg models. Sparse-QITE exhibits a controllable sparsity--accuracy trade-off while retaining strong compression even in the high-accuracy regime. In scalability experiments with respect to $D$, the active support grows much more slowly than in standard QITE and, in several regimes, approximately saturates over the domain sizes studied. evidence.abstract: Quantum imaginary-time evolution (QITE) provides a systematic route to ground-state preparation, but its cost grows rapidly with the locality $D$ of the unitary approximation, for which the local Pauli basis scales as $4^D$. We introduce Sparse-QITE, a regularized formulation that promotes compact generators, reducing the number of quantum operations and yielding circuits with fewer gates and lower depth. These results establish sparsity-promoting regularization as a route toward more resource-efficient QITE. More broadly, these results suggest that sparsity-promoting regularization may also benefit variational quantum algorithms.

title: The Physics Is the Network: Fast, Training-Free Neural Emulation
abstract: Neural emulation need not require learning a substitute for known physics. We investigate PolyNets that couple a continuous-time neural representation of polynomial dynamics with a simple recurrent network for discrete-time integration. When the governing coefficients are known, the resulting tensor graph requires no training and preserves the prescribed numerical scheme while enabling efficient hardware execution and parallel simulation. Using the one-dimensional Korteweg-de Vries equation, we compare PolyNet with CPU and GPU finite-difference Runge-Kutta solvers and three trained neural models: a state-map emulator, a physics-informed predictor, and a learned-tendency integrator. Analytical soliton solutions provide a reference for amplitude and phase errors across grid resolutions, 10^6 dispersively scaled time steps, ensembles of up to 10^4 trajectories, and varying initial amplitudes. PolyNet achieves accuracy comparable to the numerical solvers, including at amplitudes outside the learned models' training conditions. It combines this fidelity with high GPU throughput, approximately constant over the tested resolution range, and favorable ensemble scaling.

title: Trading energy for coherence in mode discrimination
abstract: Energy is arguably the main resource in classical physics; coherence is the prototypical quantum resource. In this paper, we study the interplay between these two resources in the task of optimal mode discrimination. This task, motivated by cryptography and metrology, consists of finding in which mode a signal has been encoded, for a given finite set of possible modes. After recalling that the task can be cast as a semi-definite program, we solve completely the case of two-mode discrimination under a hard energy constraint $n\leq N$. Specifically, we identify the region of modes overlap, for which the maximal energy state (the Fock state with N excitations) is the best choice for discrimination. For other overlaps, having access to coherence leads to better discrimination.

title: MakSafe: A Spatiotemporal Semantic Framework for Formal Specification and Compliance Checking of Road Vehicle Safety Rules
abstract: Scenario-based validation is essential for automated road vehicles but cannot cover the full variability of openworld traffic. We present MakSafe, a formal spatiotemporal framework for specifying and checking road vehicle safety rules through semantic zones, action-based forecasting, and trace-tree reasoning, avoiding uniform time discretization. We formalize the road network, vehicle states, and occupancy zones, then build executable rules for front-vehicle identification and timeto-collision (TTC) verification. The evaluation combines a tracedependent case study with a scalability benchmark over traffic density (N ), horizon (H), and branch factor (B). MakSafe yields branch-specific verdicts, deriving safe and unsafe outcomes from the same initial scene, and re-evaluates a scenario after a control update. A single rule check stays well below a millisecond across the reported sweep, and longer horizons slow the TTC check.

title: HyrCap: Hybrid Rank-Calibration of Action Proposals for Temporal Event Understanding
abstract: Temporal action detection in long untrimmed videos suffers from inaccurate localization and low-quality proposals, especially with sparse annotations and ambiguous boundaries. For open-ended video understanding and LLM-driven event analysis, reliable proposals connect temporal localization, event annotation, and semantic understanding. However, conventional temporal action detection (TAD) pipelines lack explicit modeling of proposal localization quality, cross-representation support, and inter-proposal relations. We propose Hybrid Rank-Calibration of Action Proposals (HyrCap), a proposal-centric query-based TAD framework for temporal event understanding. Hybrid combines complementary video features with different localization cues, while Rank-Calibration adjusts proposal ranking confidence to reflect localization reliability and candidate competition. HyrCap treats dense query-based predictions as an over-complete temporal event hypothesis space. Cross-Representation Consensus Calibration, Localization Quality Estimation, and Proposal Redundancy Suppression improve proposal ranking reliability, localization quality, and candidate discrimination. Inspired by LLMs' capabilities in fine-grained semantic recognition, event description, and reasoning, we introduce HyrCap for Semantic Action Understanding, using calibrated proposals for standard TAD and as inputs to LLM-based semantic understanding. We define a staged evaluation protocol to separately measure event localization, segment-level semantic understanding, and combined event understanding performance. Experiments on public benchmarks show that HyrCap achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics and provides a finer-grained paradigm and evaluation protocol for query-based event segmentation and annotation.

title: Online covariance estimation for stochastic gradient descent under Markovian sampling
abstract: We investigate the online overlapping batch-means covariance estimator for Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) under Markovian sampling. Under state-dependent Markovian sampling we prove a convergence rate of O(n−(1−2/α0)/8 log n), α0≥16/3 where d is the dimensionality, n denotes observations or SGD iterations, and α0 is a constant related to the mixing properties of the Markov chain. The slower mixing of the state-dependent Markov chain results in a slower rate compared to the i.i.d. case, which we illustrate with a simple example. However, under state-independent Markovian sampling, we obtain the rate O(d n−1/8) matching the best-known convergence rate for independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) data. Our analysis overcomes significant challenges arising from Markovian sampling, leading to additional error terms and complex dependencies between the blocks of the batch-means covariance estimator. Moreover, we establish the convergence rate for the first four moments of the l2 norm of the error of SGD dynamics under state-dependent Markovian data, which holds potential interest as an independent result. Numerical illustrations provide confidence intervals for SGD in linear and logistic regression models under Markovian sampling. Additionally, our method is applied to the strategic classification with logistic regression, where adversaries adaptively modify features during training to affect target class classification.

title: The impact of artificial intelligence on the purchasing decisions of different generations in clothing purchases
abstract: Nakup oblačila se danes pogosto začne, še preden potrošnik zares ve, kaj išče. Med množico izdelkov ga spremljajo priporočila, prilagojene vsebine, virtualni pomočniki in druge rešitve umetne inteligence, ki lahko spletno nakupno pot naredijo bolj osebno in usmerjeno. Vendar na drugi strani zaslona niso vsi potrošniki enaki. Pripadajo različnim generacijam, ki so odraščale v različnih časovnih in tehnoloških okoljih ter s seboj v spletni svet prinašajo svoje nakupne navade, pričakovanja in odnos do novih tehnologij. Diplomsko delo obravnava vpliv umetne inteligence na nakupno odločanje različnih generacij pri spletnem nakupovanju oblačil in nakupovanju oblačil v fizičnih trgovinah. V ospredju so babyboom generacija ter generacije X, Y in Z, pri katerih so obravnavane razlike v nakupnem vedenju, odnosu do umetne inteligence in njenem vplivu na nakupno odločanje. Posebna pozornost je namenjena oblikam umetne inteligence, s katerimi se lahko potrošnik sreča med spletnim nakupovanjem oblačil, ter njihovemu mestu v nakupnem procesu. S povezovanjem sveta mode, spletnega nakupovanja in umetne inteligence delo odpira vprašanje, ali ista tehnologija pri različnih generacijah pomeni tudi enako nakupno izkušnjo. Rezultati raziskave so pokazali, da se generacije razlikujejo predvsem pri prepoznavanju oblik umetne inteligence, pri čemer je najnižjo stopnjo prepoznavanja dosegla generacija Y, ostale generacije so prepoznale vse oblike umetne inteligence, zato je bila hipoteza H1 zavrnjena. Pri zaupanju v umetno inteligenco, njenem vplivu na pogostost nakupovanja pri vseh generacijah, ignoriranju predlogov umetne inteligence pri starejših in poenostavljanju nakupne odločitve rezultati niso potrdili zastavljenih predpostavk, zato so bile hipoteze H2, H3, H4 in H5 zavrnjene.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Selection and Collaborative Selection for Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Multiple large language models (LLMs) can independently evaluate and select candidate solutions or collaborate to determine which candidates should be selected. However, permanently relying on independent selection may fail to exploit complementary knowledge across models, whereas continuously relying on collaborative selection may introduce unnecessary communication costs, correlated judgments, conformity effects, and additional decision latency. This paper proposes Adaptive Self-Selection and Collaborative Selection (ASCCS), a framework that dynamically switches between these two selection modes according to task characteristics, candidate quality, model disagreement, estimated selection reliability, and computational cost. In self-selection mode, each model independently evaluates available candidates and produces its own selection. In collaborative-selection mode, models exchange candidate assessments, compare evidence, identify disagreements, and jointly determine a selection. A switching controller estimates the expected utility of each mode and selects the mode that best balances decision quality, robustness, latency, and resource consumption. The framework further incorporates confidence calibration, selection-history feedback, disagreement-sensitive collaboration, and an optional abstention mechanism for cases in which neither mode provides sufficient evidence. Unlike a fixed ensemble or an always-collaborative architecture, ASCCS treats the choice of selection mechanism as a dynamic decision problem. This paper formalizes the framework, presents an implementable algorithm, proposes a multi-dimensional evaluation protocol, and identifies research hypotheses for empirical investigation. The framework is designed for candidate-answer selection, reasoning-path selection, tool and model selection, planning, retrieval, and other multi-LLM decision tasks. Its effectiveness remains an empirical question to be established through controlled experiments.

title: Beyond the Black Box: A Semantic Explainable AI Framework for Transparent and Trustworthy E-
authors: Jawale Shivtej Bharat, Prof. S.V. More, Dr. H.B. Jadhav
abstract: Artificial intelligence has become an important part of modern e-commerce, supporting product recommendations, search ranking, customer-review analysis, and personalized shopping experiences. Despite these benefits, customers often receive recommendations without understanding the reasons behind them. This lack of transparency can make it difficult to distinguish a genuinely relevant suggestion from one influenced by popularity, incomplete information, or commercial priorities. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) offers a way to make these decisions more understandable. However, explanations are useful only when they communicate relevant evidence accurately rather than simply presenting convincing language. This paper examines the relationship between XAI, semantic analysis, and transparent decision-making in e-commerce, with particular attention to research trends during 2024, 2025, and 2026. It proposes a conceptual framework that connects customer preferences, product attributes, review sentiment, recommendation models, and evidence-based explanations. The framework is designed to explain why a product may be relevant, which features support the recommendation, and where conflicting information remains. The paper also discusses explanation faithfulness, customer privacy, review reliability, fairness, and the limitations of language-model-generated explanations. Its contribution is a practical design approach for connecting recommendation decisions with verifiable semantic evidence. Future implementation and user testing are required to determine whether this approach improves customer understanding and decision quality in real shopping environments

title: A Dual-Loop Intelligent Teaching Assistant System for Adaptive Web-Based Teaching and Decision Support
abstract: Web-based technologies often fail to fundamentally reshape teaching processes, despite their ubiquity. This study presents a dual-loop intelligent teaching assistant system that integrates natural language processing-driven intent recognition and sentiment analysis within a human-in-the-loop framework. Unlike systems prioritizing pure automation, this study's architecture dynamically routes complex queries to instructors via a visual decision-support dashboard, balancing real-time responsiveness with pedagogical nuance. Empirical results in higher education reveal that while interaction efficiency improved significantly, user satisfaction depended nonlinearly on technical accuracy, heavily influenced by notification strategies and emergent student behaviors, like reverse engineering the bot. These findings underscore the need to evolve web-based tools from static utilities into adaptive sociotechnical ecosystems that actively support both learner autonomy and instructor decision-making.

title: RIDI-REAL-UPDATES-v1: Individual correctness changes across released model updates and prediction from frozen fragility
abstract: Prospective, not yet executed. This study tests whether six pinned incumbent-to-successor language-model releases produce individual-question correctness changes even when aggregate benchmark performance is favourable, and whether the previously frozen RIDI-PREDICT-v1 fragility score F_B predicts those changes. The panel contains 800 questions (Natural Questions 250, HotpotQA 250, FEVER 300) with the byte-identical registered BM25 top-10 reference contexts from OSF xrzp5. No passage exchange will be performed. Twelve pinned instruction-tuned models will each run in main (single-question generation) and replay-floor (fixed batches of 16) conditions: 24 model-by-condition units. The optional API pair is excluded. Decoding, scoring, retries, blinding, model revisions and audit procedures are detailed in the attached protocol. A unit is retried only after a documented technical failure; no successful output or partial batch is reused. The full set of units must terminate before opening answers or performing scientific analysis. Prespecified endpoints and decisions: equal-benchmark-weight accuracy difference Delta, aggregate accept flags C0 and C1, per-question correctness disagreement D, per-model replay floors and excess E; H1 requires the 95% lower bound for E > 2 percentage points in at least four of six pairs and every C0-accepted pair; H2 tests pooled AUC of F_B with support at AUC >= .60 and 95% lower bound > .55; H3 tests an adjusted logistic association with specified covariates and prespecified separation/Firth handling, with odds-ratio lower bound > 1.3. The plan specifies 100,000 joint within-benchmark paired bootstrap resamples (seed 20261013). S1-S6 and independent auditing are also specified. Prior knowledge and limitations: P8 remains INCOMPLETE and is neither rerun nor rescued; RIDI-PREDICT's AUC results and a disclosed post-run analysis recovery are known. F_B values were known to the author; Qwen3-8B overlaps the predictors and is not an unseen model, and archived Qwen3 reference correctness is available for reproduction checks only. 'Accepted' is a prespecified study rule, not a claim about a vendor's actual release decision. No scientific generation in this new study has begun.

Prior knowledge and limitations: P8 remains INCOMPLETE and is neither rerun nor rescued; RIDI-PREDICT's AUC results and a disclosed post-run analysis recovery are known. F_B values were known to the author; Qwen3-8B overlaps the predictors and is not an unseen model, and archived Qwen3 reference correctness is available for reproduction checks only. 'Accepted' is a prespecified study rule, not a claim about a vendor's actual release decision. No scientific generation in this new study has begun.

title: Python Using GPT-5 and Gemini
abstract: Python Using GPT‑5 and Gemini provides a practical, up‑to‑date guide that combines solid Python programming skills with real‑world integration of today’s leading large language models (LLMs). This book teaches essential Python techniques while showing readers exactly how to connect and use GPT‑5, Google Gemini, Claude, Grok, Perplexity, and other major 2026 models in their daily work. Readers will gain a strong foundation in Python data structures, comprehensions, generators, regular expressions, and object‑oriented programming. This book then moves into detailed coverage of GPT‑5 (including GPT‑5.4 and GPT‑5.3 Instant), Gemini 3.1, Claude Mythos, and Opus 4.6, along with practical Python code samples for chatbots, tool calling, data analysis, graphics generation, and integration with PowerPoint and Excel. Additional chapters explore LLM benchmarks, deceptive behaviors such as alignment faking and scheming, military AI applications, and comparisons between the major models, giving readers clear insight into their relative strengths and limitations. This book is written for intermediate Python developers, data scientists, technical professionals, and anyone who wants to move beyond basic prompting and build production‑ready applications that effectively combine Python with the latest generation of LLMs.

title: Web X.0 and intelligent automation beyond Web 3.0
abstract: This chapter examines the role of intelligent automation within the evolving paradigm of Web X.0, with particular emphasis on artificial intelligence (AI)-powered automation, machine learning, and predictive analytics. It analyzes how web-based user experiences are being enhanced through AI-driven personalized search engines, automated customer support services, and intelligent digital assistants. Furthermore, the chapter addresses ethical and socio-technical issues associated with these technologies, including algorithmic bias, data privacy and protection, and the implications for the future of work in an AI-intensive web ecosystem. Finally, the chapter evaluates interoperability and standardization aspects in relation to World Wide Web Consortium recommendations, decentralized identity frameworks, and mechanisms for cross-platform data compatibility.

title: Sign Betting for Misspecified Regression: Variance Adaptivity and Optimal Approximation
abstract: We study bounded regression under model misspecification, evaluating a function $f$ by its $L_1(P_X)$ distance to the conditional mean $η(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$, rather than the standard $L_2(P_X)$. This $L_1$ metric is natural for downstream decision problems such as bandits and reinforcement learning. We analyze the min--max estimator of Baraud & Maillard (2025), which we call \emph{sign-betting regression}. Our main results show that sign-betting regression achieves high-probability $L_1$ oracle inequalities under misspecification. Under realizability, our bound adapts to the average conditional variance and recovers the variance-adaptive rate of Li et al. (2026). We further characterize the optimal universal approximation factor for proper learning by showing that sign betting achieves factor 3, while no proper learner can satisfy a distribution-free, high-probability $L_1$ oracle inequality with a universal approximation factor strictly below 3. We extend the upper-bound analysis beyond finite classes and complement the theory with experiments in synthetic and real-world model-selection tasks.

title: Object Pose from 2-D to 3-D Point and Line Correspondences
abstract: In this paper we present a method for optimally estimating the rotation and translation between a camera and a 3-D object from point and/or line correspondences. First we devise an error function and second we show how to minimize this error function. The quadratic nature of this function is made possible by representing rotation and translation with a dual number quaternion. We provide a detailed account of the computational aspects of a trust-region optimization method. This method compares favourably with Newton's method which has extensively been used to solve the problem at hand, with Faugeras-Toscani linear method [6] for calibrating a camera, and with the Levenberg-Marquardt non-linear optimization method. Finally we present some experimental results which demonstrate the robustness of our method with respect to image noise and matching errors.

title: Learning Optimal Classification Trees Robust to Distribution Shifts
abstract: We consider the problem of learning classification trees that are robust to distribution shifts between training and testing/deployment data. This problem arises frequently in high stakes settings such as public health and social work where data is often collected using self-reported surveys which are highly sensitive to e.g., the framing of the questions, the time when and place where the survey is conducted, and the level of comfort the interviewee has in sharing information with the interviewer. We propose a method for learning optimal robust classification trees based on mixed-integer robust optimization technology. In particular, we demonstrate that the problem of learning an optimal robust tree can be cast as a single-stage mixed-integer robust optimization problem with a highly nonlinear and discontinuous objective. We reformulate this problem equivalently as a two-stage linear robust optimization problem for which we devise a tailored solution procedure based on constraint generation. We evaluate the performance of our approach on numerous publicly available datasets, and compare the performance to a regularized, non-robust optimal tree. We show an increase of up to 12.48 percentage points in worst-case accuracy and of up to 4.85 percentage points in average-case accuracy across several datasets and distribution shifts from using our robust solution in comparison to the non-robust one.

title: Stochastic Risk Simulator: discrete-event multiagent simulation with bounded-memory PATL verification
abstract: Stochastic Risk Simulator is a general, domain-independent framework for evaluating risk in systems where many agents decide under uncertainty and against one another. It combines a discrete-event simulation of stochastic multiagent systems with exact strategic verification in probabilistic alternating-time temporal logic with bounded-memory, observation-based strategies (PATL_b). The framework follows the principle simulate to reach, solve to verify. The discrete-event engine executes a scenario and freezes the global state whenever an agent enters a state declared critical. From each snapshot, a bounded game between a coalition and its adversaries is solved exactly: branch probabilities are exact masses rather than samples, adversaries are unrestricted, and the coalition has imperfect information. Each risk question therefore returns a deterministic worst-case value, a verdict and the class of the strategy that attains it. Scenarios are specified entirely as JSON files validated against schemas (agents, environments, automata, distributions, events and coalition predicates); the engine contains no domain logic. Contents of this record- Source code of the simulation engine and the verifier (Python).- JSON schemas for scenario specification.- The case study of the accompanying article: liquidity runway of a startup with eight agent types, 111 agent instances, twenty-two automata and twelve predicates, in four macroeconomic regimes (Bull, Base, Bear, Crisis).- An automated test suite of 71 tests, including twenty-six games whose value is computed in closed form.- Documentation with the exact commands to reproduce the experiment of the article. The raw output (198,302 verifications) is not included; it is regenerated exactly from the configuration and the recorded seeds, and the documentation lists the number of verification rows expected in each regime. Accompanying articleKuzmanovski Reyes, B. Y., and Gavira Durón, N. Simulate to Reach, Solve to Verify: A General Risk Evaluation Framework via Multiagent Discrete-Event Simulation and Exact Strategic Verification. Submitted to ACM Transactions on Modeling and Computer Simulation. The work derives from the undergraduate thesis in Mathematics of the first author (Facultad de Ciencias, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, 2026), supervised by Dr. Nora Gavira Durón. title: FUZZYBOOST-HET: a competence-learned fuzzy-integral ensemble for stable feature selection
abstract: Replication bundle for FUZZYBOOST-HET, a feature selector that runs five heterogeneous selectors (XGBoost gain, random-forest impurity, mutual information, ANOVA F, RFE with random forest) over stratified bootstrap resamples of the training fold and aggregates their per-feature top-k membership profiles with a Choquet integral over a lambda-fuzzy measure whose densities are each selector's measured nested-cross-validation competence. Contents: fuzzyboost/ - the Python package (HET selector, FS/RFE companions, lambda-fuzzy measure, Sugeno and Choquet integrals, OWA, fuzzy TOPSIS, fuzzy c-means); scripts/ - every benchmark harness, the aggregation/competence/RFE ablations and the analysis layer that regenerates the reported statistics from the raw CSVs; data/ - a frozen mirror of 20 Penn Machine Learning Benchmarks (PMLB) datasets; results/ - raw per-cell result CSVs (20 datasets x 10 methods x 5 feature fractions) and the analysis outputs. Protocol: stratified 5-fold CV, random_state 42, selection strictly inside the training fold; balanced accuracy of a 100-tree class-balanced random forest; stability as mean pairwise Jaccard overlap between fold supports. Headline result over 96 paired cells: accuracy parity with XGBoost gain selection (+0.0043, Wilcoxon p = 0.342) with a significantly more stable support (+0.138 Jaccard, p = 8.5e-12). Five negative results are included, not suppressed. Install: pip install -r requirements.txt (Python 3.11+); full reproduction order in README.txt. Code: MIT; data and figures: CC BY 4.0.

title: Parallel-World Adaptive Routing for Large Language Models: A Unified Framework for Adaptive Self-Routing, Collaborative Routing, and Cross-Model Coordination
abstract: Large language model (LLM) routing enables computational systems to select appropriate models, reasoning strategies, tools, or execution pathways for different inputs. Existing approaches have investigated adaptive model selection, cost-aware routing, model cascades, and multi-agent collaboration. However, a routing architecture that explicitly combines multiple parallel routing worlds derived from the same underlying model with heterogeneous external models, while adaptively switching between independent self-routing and collaborative routing, remains a promising direction for systematic investigation. This paper proposes Parallel-World Adaptive Routing (PWAR), a framework in which multiple routing worlds originate from the same base LLM but develop distinct routing policies, task preferences, exploration strategies, or decision criteria. Each world can independently select an execution pathway through adaptive self-routing or participate in collaborative routing with other worlds and heterogeneous external LLMs. A meta-routing controller determines when independent routing is sufficient, when cross-world coordination is beneficial, and when heterogeneous model collaboration is warranted. The framework incorporates task difficulty estimation, uncertainty assessment, resource constraints, routing-policy diversity, feedback-based adaptation, and outcome-aware coordination. Unlike a fixed routing architecture, PWAR treats the routing mode itself as an adaptive decision. It therefore distinguishes between selecting a destination and deciding how routing decisions should be produced. The paper formalizes the framework, presents its operational workflow and optimization objectives, and proposes an experimental protocol for evaluating effectiveness, computational cost, latency, robustness, and routing diversity. No experimental results are claimed in this conceptual paper. The proposed framework is intended to provide a testable research foundation for adaptive routing across parallel instances of a shared model and heterogeneous model ecosystems.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Parallel-World Self-Correction and Mutual Correction for Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate incorrect, incomplete, or internally inconsistent responses. Self-correction allows a model to inspect and revise its own outputs, whereas mutual correction enables multiple model instances or heterogeneous models to identify and address one another's errors. However, relying exclusively on either mechanism may limit the diversity of corrective perspectives, increase computational costs, or reinforce existing mistakes. This paper proposes Adaptive Parallel-World Self-Correction and Mutual Correction (APSMC), a unified framework in which multiple LLMs dynamically switch between independent self-correction and collaborative mutual correction according to the observed characteristics of their outputs and the estimated benefits of further interaction. The framework introduces parallel worlds, defined as independently maintained corrective trajectories generated by the same underlying model under different correction objectives, prompts, reasoning constraints, or contextual perspectives. Each trajectory performs self-correction before selectively exchanging information with other trajectories. An adaptive controller determines whether the system should continue independent correction, initiate pairwise mutual correction, activate group-level correction, or terminate the process. The framework also supports heterogeneous LLMs that participate in correction without belonging to the same parallel-world group. Unlike fixed self-correction and permanently collaborative architectures, APSMC treats the choice between independent and collaborative correction as a dynamic decision-making problem. This paper formalizes the framework, presents a correction-selection algorithm, defines evaluation metrics, and proposes an experimental protocol for assessing accuracy, correction reliability, diversity, computational efficiency, and resistance to collective errors. The framework is a research proposal; its effectiveness and novelty relative to existing methods require systematic empirical validation.

title: Development and multi-database validation of machine learning models for 28-day mortality prediction in ICU patients with COPD and pulmonary hypertension
abstract: Background Early mortality prediction in critically ill patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) coexisting pulmonary hypertension (PH) remains challenging, particularly because prediction models developed in intensive care unit (ICU) database may not perform consistently across other healthcare systems. Methods This retrospective multicenter study employed two large-scale databases to establish and validate ML models for predicting early mortality in ICU patients with COPD and PH. The MIMIC-IV database served as the model-development cohort (2555 patients), with external validation conducted on eICU CRD (292 patients) database. Six ML algorithms were adopted: Random Forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Logistic Regression (LR), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Artificial Neural Network (ANN). The baseline variables were screened to identify potential predictors via least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (Lasso) regression. Model interpretability was evaluated via SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis. Results The overall cohort consisted of 2,847 ICU patients with COPD and PH. Twelve consistently crucial clinical features were identified, including acute kidney injury, pneumonia, age, weight, heart rate, red blood cell distribution width (RDW), white blood cell (WBC), anion gap, chloride, creatinine, base excess, potential of hydrogen (pH). The Random Forest algorithm achieved the optimal performance, with a training Area Under Curve (AUC) of 0.938, internal validation AUC of 0.748, and eICU CRD external validation AUC of 0.800. SHAP analysis indicated that acute kidney injury was the most influential predictor, followed by base excess and RDW. Additionally, a web tool was developed in this study to facilitate the application of early death risk prediction in clinical practice. Conclusions This study is the multi-database validation of ML models for early mortality prediction in ICU patients with COPD and PH. The Random Forest model integrated with SHAP interpretability offers a reliable tool for clinical decision-making support, with consistent validity verified across two databases, including our internal validation cohort. This work provides a decision support tool to assist in identifying high-risk individuals within this complex comorbid population, and establishes a foundation for future studies with a more dynamic and personalized prognostic approach.

title: TGrasp6D: Task-Informed Vision-Language Priors and Pose Refinement enable Zero-Shot Task-Oriented 6DoF Grasping
abstract: Task-Oriented Grasping (TOG) has emerged as an important skill for purposeful robotic manipulation. Given the task of using a knife to "slice bread," a robot must choose to grasp from the handle, whereas for "hand[ing] the knife over," it is preferable for the handle to remain unobstructed for safe handoff. Current approaches for TOG either focus on 2D planar grasping, remain limited by their reliance on task-agnostic grasp generators, or are constrained by reliance on finite, manually-annotated, task-specific grasp datasets that cannot cover all possible grasp-task pairs. To that end, we present TGrasp6D, a vision-language based approach for generating task-oriented 6DoF grasps in a zero-shot manner. Given a task and a single RGB-D image of an associated object, TGrasp6D reasons about the appropriate semantic affordance for the given task and object geometry to produce an initial task- informed prior. This generated prior is further refined via 6DoF pose optimization for collision avoidance while preserving task consistency. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art success rate of 94% on the TaskGrasp dataset, with the best baseline at 74%. evidence.title: TGrasp6D: Task-Informed Vision-Language Priors and Pose Refinement enable Zero-Shot Task-Oriented 6DoF Grasping
evidence.abstract: Task-Oriented Grasping (TOG) has emerged as an important skill for purposeful robotic manipulation. Given the task of using a knife to "slice bread," a robot must choose to grasp from the handle, whereas for "hand[ing] the knife over," it is preferable for the handle to remain unobstructed for safe handoff. Current approaches for TOG either focus on 2D planar grasping, remain limited by their reliance on task-agnostic grasp generators, or are constrained by reliance on finite, manually-annotated, task-specific grasp datasets that cannot cover all possible grasp-task pairs. To that end, we present TGrasp6D, a vision-language based approach for generating task-oriented 6DoF grasps in a zero-shot manner. Given a task and a single RGB-D image of an associated object, TGrasp6D reasons about the appropriate semantic affordance for the given task and object geometry to produce an initial task- informed prior. This generated prior is further refined via 6DoF pose optimization for collision avoidance while preserving task consistency. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art success rate of 94% on the TaskGrasp dataset, with the best baseline at 74%. We also deploy our approach on a Franka Research 3 robot to demonstrate zero-shot generalization to real world objects

title: Tulva: Practical Asynchronous Threshold FHE
abstract: We present Tulva, a practical threshold FHE scheme which equips a base FHE scheme with an asynchronous threshold decryption mechanism in a modular way. Our scheme simultaneously (1) is compatible with virtually any base FHE scheme and leaves its ciphertexts unchanged apart from an appended random tag, (2) supports a wide range of threshold profiles $(t,K)$ and ring degrees $\geq 256$ with 6-25 bits partial decryption per plaintext bit, and (3) achieves security in the presence of partial decryption queries on challenge ciphertexts based on the standard LWE assumption. We provide an open-source implementation, benchmark its threshold decryption performance and evaluate the end-to-end costs for typical privacy-preserving Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) use cases. For 16-out-of-512 threshold and a publicly preprocessed ciphertext, computing secret-dependent partial decryption and public share combination requires only 3.7 ms and 0.5 ms, respectively, on commodity hardware. Compared with the state-of-the-art synchronous scheme [Zyskind et al., CCS'25], we replace their ciphertext-independent yet interactive preparation of secret-correlated randomness with a public, ciphertext-dependent 0.5 s preprocessing step, eliminate interaction in the online phase while maintaining similar decryption time on the same machine, and support 32$\times$ more total users.

title: Exact Cut Complexity of Equal-Length Proportional Cake Cutting
abstract: We study proportional cake cutting under an equal-length constraint, where each of $n$ agents must receive a bundle of length exactly $1/n$ that is worth at least $1/n$ to that agent. Our main result determines the exact worst-case number of cuts needed to guarantee such an allocation, namely $2n-2$ for every $n$. This improves on the previously known quadratic upper bound. The proof combines the constrained necklace-splitting theorem with a recursive assignment argument based on Hall's theorem. The same bound extends to the stronger requirement of envy-freeness when $n$ is a prime power, and an $O(n^{1.525})$ upper bound holds for arbitrary $n$. We then ask whether such allocations can be computed. We first show that no deterministic protocol in the Robertson--Webb model terminates after finitely many queries on every instance and always returns an exact equal-length proportional allocation, even for two agents with identical valuations. For every $\varepsilon>0$, however, $O(n^2/\varepsilon)$ queries suffice to produce an allocation in which every agent receives a bundle of length exactly $1/n$ and value at least $1/n-\varepsilon$, again using at most $2n-2$ cuts. Finally, we augment the Robertson--Webb model with two-knife queries. We show that recursive balanced halving attains the optimal bound of $2n-2$ cuts when $n$ is a power of two. For arbitrary $n$, we give a procedure using $O(n\log n)$ cuts.

title: HankelKANet: Lightweight Path Loss Estimation via Physics-Inspired Hankel Convolution
abstract: Accurate path loss (PL) estimation is essential for wireless network planning and optimization. This paper proposes HankelKANet, a lightweight physics-inspired network for PL estimation that structurally embeds electromagnetic propagation characteristics into the neural architecture. Built on a single residual UNet backbone, the proposed model integrates urban layout features with a convolutional Kolmogorov-Arnold network(KAN). Specifically, the convolutional kernels are parameterized by the radial amplitudes of the zeroth- and first-order Hankel functions. This formulation acts as a physics-inspired nonlinear distance encoding, enabling the network to capture dominant attenuation characteristics directly without requiring additional physics-based loss terms. Experimental results demonstrate that HankelKANet achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and efficiency on both the simulated RadioMapSeer dataset and the real-world Huawei RSRPSet. Compared with the leading baseline, PEFNet, it reduces the parameter count by 78% and lowers the RMSE by 16.96% on the simulated data, while further exhibiting robust cross-dataset transferability and high data efficiency during target-domain adaptation. To interpret these empirical gains, we mathematically establish a parameter-conditional spatial gradient bound. Using discrete Dirichlet energy (DDE) and Jacobian sensitivity heatmaps, we empirically verify that this physical encoding intrinsically constrains the network's spatial derivatives. This structural smoothness effectively eliminates non-physical spatial ripples, preventing overfitting to simulator artifacts and serving as the fundamental driver for robust real world generalization.

title: Active Generative Simulation: Meta-Learning What to Simulate for Sim-and-Real Policy Co-Training
abstract: Sim-and-real co-training is an effective way to scale robot learning by augmenting limited real-world demonstrations with simulation data. However, existing approaches typically treat simulators as fixed data sources, relying on uniform generation, offline retrieval, or manual parameter alignment by domain experts. We formulate \textit{Active Generative Simulation}: optimizing a simulator's data-generation distribution to maximize downstream real-world performance. To solve this problem, we propose MetaGenSim, a meta-learning framework that trains an auxiliary rater network via meta-gradients to automatically discover high-utility data-generation distributions within a user-specified simulation parameter space, without manual parameter alignment. Across simulation and real-world manipulation tasks, MetaGenSim outperforms uniform generation and retrieval baselines, achieves a 150% relative improvement in real-world full-task success over uniform generation, and matches expert manual alignment. We further show that distributions curated with a lightweight proxy policy transfer to VLA fine-tuning, and that MetaGenSim can exploit partial alignment through atomic skill stitching and object-receptacle composition when exact sim-and-real task alignment is unavailable. Project website: https://meta-gensim.github.io

title: Federated Distillation: A Survey
abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without centralizing clients’ raw data, but parameter exchange can impose substantial communication costs and usually requires compatible model architectures. Federated distillation (FD) instead transfers predictive or intermediate knowledge through knowledge distillation (KD), which can support heterogeneous models and reduce communication in suitable settings. These benefits are not automatic: their magnitude depends on the transmitted knowledge, reference data, communication schedule, and threat model. This survey provides a challenge-centered synthesis of FD. We first formalize a representative public-data, response-based FD protocol and then organize existing methods by the FL challenges they address, including data, system, and model heterogeneity, client drift, catastrophic forgetting, communication cost, and privacy risk. We further review applications in industrial engineering, computer vision, natural language processing, and healthcare, including recent federated adaptation of large language models. Finally, we identify five research priorities: richer transferred knowledge, joint treatment of interacting forms of heterogeneity, communication-aware distillation, threat-model-driven privacy protection, and standardized theory, benchmarks, and evaluation.

title: Consumer trust in ai-generated advertisement content
abstract: Diplomsko delo obravnava področje sodobnega oglaševanja s poudarkom na vplivu generativne umetne inteligence na zaupanje potrošnikov. Problem izhaja iz hitrega napredka tehnologij UI, ki podjetjem omogočajo avtomatizirano ustvarjanje naprednih oglasnih besedil, slik in videoposnetkov, medtem ko se pri potrošnikih pojavljajo skepticizem in etični pomisleki. Delo temelji na teoretični opredelitvi koncepta zaupanja in k temu sodečih pojmov, empirično pa analiziramo odziv slovenskih potrošnikov na konkretni UI-generiran video oglas z uporabo prilagojene merske lestvice ADTRUST. V raziskavi ugotavljamo zadržano in nevtralno splošno zaupanje potrošnikov v UI-generirane oglasne vsebine. Potrošniki najvišje ocenjujejo čustvene, estetske in tehnične vidike oglasov, bistveno nižje pa resničnost in pripravljenost za sprejemanje nakupnih odločitev na njihovi podlagi. Nadaljnji rezultati potrjujejo, da splošni pozitiven odnos do UI vpliva na višjo stopnjo zaupanja v UI-oglase, medtem ko demografske značilnosti, kot so spol, starost in izobrazba, ne pokažejo statistično pomembnih razlik v stopnji zaupanja.

title: Flatland: The Adventures of Gradient Descent with Large Step Sizes
abstract: The training of neural networks often entails objective functions that are not globally L-smooth. For these functions, it is both theroetically and practically difficult to reply to the question: what is the largest possible step size that ensures the convergence of gradient descent (GD)? We address this longstanding open question in deep learning by providing a unifying definition of "large" step sizes that requires only local Lipschitz (or even Hölder) continuity of the gradient. We design first-order adaptive methods that provably yield large step sizes and show that they operate at the edge of stability (EoS) right from the start of the training. In particular, the loss decreases nonmonotonically and the product between the step size and sharpness, i.e., the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian, stays above the EoS threshold of 2 throughout training. Using our method, we are also able to minimize the sharpness all the way down to its global minimum. Contrary to expectation, we find that encountering globally-flat regions too early in the training may both slow down convergence and jeopardize the generalization ability of the network. Exploiting a self-stabilization argument, we allow GD to enter slightly sharper valleys and turn unsuccessful training runs into very successful ones.

title: Antigravity HFS: Memory-Resident Debian Kernel & Loopback Hole-Buffer Guard against Trailing Viruses
abstract: Release Version 1.0.0 of the HFS (Hole-buffer File System) autonomous architecture. Combines a memory-resident Debian 12/Linux 6.12+ kernel (toram), kernel RAM disk (/dev/ram0), loopback sparse container (hfs.img on /dev/loop0), and cryptographic SHA-256 hole-buffer and sector slack space hashing to detect and neutralize trailing viruses.

title: The Great Enterprise LLM Decoupling: Weight-Space IP Contagion, Orthogonal Backprop-Burn Infeasibility, Hardware-Enforced No-Learn Attestation, and Mandatory Third-Party Model Purge under Delaware Caremark Standards
abstract: Abstract: Global enterprise technology stacks—most notably Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) constituents and sovereign cloud operators—are executing an unprecedented structural purge of third-party frontier Large Language Models (LLMs), epitomized by the enterprise decoupling from external black-box providers ("Goodbye, Claude"). While superficially interpreted as cost optimization or routine vendor consolidation, this monograph proves that the decoupling is driven by an acute, existential legal and mathematical crisis: Weight-Space Intellectual Property (IP) Contagion and Fiduciary Liability Transmission. Building upon our forensic analysis of cross-border training data laundering (Project Panama, Record 23311531) and our Biological & Algorithmic IP Protection Covenants (NLL-v1.0-2026, Record 23358010), we establish four foundational results: (1) We formulate the Weight-Space Contagion Theorem, proving via non-diagonal Hessian cross-derivative coupling ($\nabla^2_{\theta} \mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}$) that copyrighted works and sovereign trade secrets ingested during pre-training or fine-tuning cannot be surgically "unlearned" post-hoc without inducing catastrophic perplexity collapse (Orthogonal Backprop-Burn Infeasibility); (2) We model Transitive Enterprise Contamination, demonstrating how API outputs, synthetic distillation, and IDE code completions transmit copyright taint ($\phi_{\text{taint}} \to 100\%$) directly into proprietary corporate repositories; (3) We design a Hardware-Enforced Zero-Gradient Attestation Architecture ($\pi_{\text{no-learn}}$) utilizing Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) and recursive STARK proofs over the 64-bit Goldilocks field ($\mathbb{F}_p, p = 2^{64} - 2^{32} + 1$) to guarantee mathematically that enterprise inference and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) execute with strictly zero weight updates ($\nabla_{\theta} W \equiv \mathbf{0}$); and (4) We prove under Delaware General Corporation Law (Caremark standard) and SEC Rule 15c3-5 / Item 1.05 disclosure mandates that corporate boards retaining un-auditable third-party LLMs after receiving constructive notice of supply-chain IP laundering face personal, non-exculpated liability for bad-faith breach of the duty of loyalty. Finally, we codify a 4-stage Enterprise Decoupling Protocol transitioning global infrastructure from contaminated black-box APIs to sovereign, clean-room verified in-house AI stacks.

title: Matched-Capacity Comparison of Additive and Multiplicative Neural Network Surrogates for Response Prediction of Steel Roof Trusses
authors: Dr. V. K. Verma Deepak Kulyal
abstract: ABSTRACT Repeated finite element analyses account for most of the computational effort in designing steel roof trusses, and neural network surrogates can remove much of this burden. However, the influence of the neuron model on surrogate quality is seldom examined under controlled conditions. In this work, an additive multilayer perceptron (MLP) and a multiplicative neuron model (MNM) of nearly equal size (211 and 196 trainable parameters, respectively) are compared. Training data were drawn from a parametric STAAD.Pro database of 46,140 Fink, Howe, Pratt and Warren trusses checked against IS 800:2007, in which non-compliant designs were deliberately retained. Using nineteen input variables, each network estimated eight continuous responses together with a binary pass/fail design status. On held-out test data, the mean coefficient of determination of the MLP ranged from 0.942 to 0.946 across the four profiles, compared with 0.700 to 0.775 for the MNM. The corresponding mean absolute percentage errors were 11–17 % and 26–37 %. Total weight was the most accurately estimated response (MLP R² ≥ 0.964), while the maximum utilisation ratio was the least accurate (R² ≈ 0.80–0.83), because the critical member shifts from one region of the design space to another. In pass/fail classification, the false negative rate of the MLP was 0.074–0.213, against 0.210–0.608 for the MNM. Since the MNM used a bounded geometric-mean aggregation and had marginally fewer parameters, its weaker performance is traced to the multiplicative form itself, which is poorly suited to the largely additive behaviour of truss responses. The MLP is therefore recommended as the surrogate, with its utilisation predictions regarded as the least reliable output. Key words: neural network surrogate, steel roof truss, multiplicative neuron model, multilayer perceptron, IS 800:2007, STAAD.Pro.

title: New PV output power forecasting approach using solar spectrum and deep learning for ultra-short time horizon
abstract: Accurate ultra-short-term forecasting of photovoltaic output is essential for improving the reliability and stability of solar energy systems. However, many existing forecasting methods rely primarily on irradiance-based features and do not fully exploit the information contained in the solar spectrum. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a two-stage approach to ultra-short-term forecasting of PV output current using solar spectral information. In the first stage, solar spectral irradiance is forecasted, while in the second stage, the PV array current is estimated to use the predicted spectra and a multilayer perceptron (MLP) regression model. The proposed method is compared with three alternative forecasting schemes. Firstly, a model based on statistical features of solar irradiance, including the moving-average clear-sky index (CSI ma ) and moving-average variance (σ ma ). Secondly, a model combining CSI ma , σ ma , irradiance, and spectral data. Thirdly, a model using irradiance, the white-to-total ratio ( wtr ), and sky images. Experiments were conducted using data collected in October 2025, and forecasting performance was evaluated for horizons of 1, 5, 10, 15, 30, and 60 minutes using R² score, MAE, MSE, and RMSE. The results show that forecasting accuracy decreases as the prediction horizon increases, with R² decreasing and error metrics increasing across all models. Nevertheless, the proposed spectral two-stage MLP-based approach achieves the best performance, with an R² of 0.971 for a 1-minute horizon and strong explanatory power (R² ≈ 0.87) for horizons up to 15 minutes. These results indicate that incorporating solar spectral information can significantly enhance the accuracy of ultra-short-term PV current forecasting.

title: Bayesian Learning to Select Fair Classifiers
abstract: Evaluations of classifiers (AI or human or agents) often assume a batch setting in which every agent produces labels on every example in a test set, which can be expensive or impractical in many contexts. This motivates online policies that adaptively select agents to query as examples arrive and update policies as outcomes are observed. We study the problem of selecting, in an online stream, the agent that best balances (i) predictive performance and (ii) subgroup fairness of a sensitive attribute, and that allows for delayed observations of true class labels. We formulate this as a Bayesian multi-armed bandit problem using Thompson Sampling, explicitly balancing accuracy and fairness. We conduct empirical evaluations on real-world datasets spanning problems involving tabular classifiers, large language models, and human labelers, demonstrating substantial reductions in regret relative to baselines. Our theoretical contributions include guarantees on the performance of the selected agent that incorporate both the accuracy and fairness aspects of the problem.

title: Controlling the latency in temporal coded spiking models for neuromorphic datasets
abstract: Exploiting temporal information in datasets with high temporal dependencies (such as spoken keyword recognition) by spiking models is still an open problem. Promising frameworks include Time-To-First coding (TTFS) and the inclusion of synaptic delays into learning. In TTFS, neurons are forced to spike at most once, forcing the network to found its learning on the spiking times of neurons rather than their spiking rate. Some models use the TTFS framework to directly compute the spiking time of Integrate-and-Fire (IF) or Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons. However, most models built in the TTFS framework have not been tested against datasets containing temporal information. Little is known about the latency of these models on temporal datasets, where the latency is the time taken by the network to correctly classify a sample. In this work, we study the behaviour of Delay Neural Networks (DeNN) models, i.e. models that directly compute the spiking time of neurons by bypassing the membrane potential and thresholding mechanisms of spiking neurons. We show how to analytically control their latency, and empirically study the latency-accuracy tradeoff in a dynamic temporal dataset.

title: Spectral World Renderer: Unified 3D Hyperspectral Unmixing
abstract: Cameras and the foundation models built on them recognize what a 3D scene contains, but not what it is made of: surfaces of the same colour can be different materials. Hyperspectral unmixing explains each spectrum as a mixture of material signatures, yet in 3D it is applied to rendered images after the views are composited, or tied to slow implicit fields, and no multi-view data with known composition exist to check the result. We present the Spectral World Renderer (SWR), which unifies world generation and unmixing. A coding agent builds executable 3D worlds that are rendered with measured spectra, so every hyperspectral image comes with exact labels and sub-pixel proportions; the resulting SWR-Bench provides eight indoor and outdoor worlds in which decompositions can be verified. SWR then unmixes inside rendering: each Gaussian of a compact 3D representation is decoded into material abundances before compositing, so one render yields spectra and material maps, and any surface can be queried by material name, a clicked pixel or a reference spectrum. Without material labels, SWR identifies materials best in all eight worlds, has the best mean PSNR on real captures, trains 3.7-12.9x faster than unmixing baselines, renders 34.9 labelled views/s and separates same-coloured materials.

title: The use of artificial intelligence in the clothing industry
abstract: Diplomsko delo obravnava uporabo umetne inteligence v oblačilni industriji s poudarkom na personalizaciji uporabniške izkušnje. Predstavljene so rešitve, kot so priporočilni sistemi, predlogi velikosti, virtualno pomerjanje, personalizirano oglaševanje, napovedovanje trendov in upravljanje zalog. Rezultati anketne raziskave, v kateri je sodelovalo 140 oseb, so pokazali statistično značilno pozitivno povezanost med uporabo pripomočkov umetne inteligence in zaznano personalizacijo uporabniške izkušnje ter med zaznano personalizacijo in lojalnostjo potrošnikov. Ugotovljeno je bilo tudi, da imajo funkcije umetne inteligence pri nakupnem odločanju predvsem podporno, ne pa odločilne vloge. Učinkovitost umetne inteligence je tako odvisna predvsem od uporabnosti rešitev, kakovosti podatkov, transparentnosti njihove uporabe in zaupanja potrošnikov.
